chapter_theme: Sages teach the Vidyadhara king that deeds sprung from a lack of true knowledge bind beings through births until they take refuge at the Lord's feet and hold true seeing, knowledge and conduct, whose end is a state of unfailing bliss; the king goes home, and his young daughter takes the Chakravalam vow and worships the Lord on the hill.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge; here called by his land and arms, not by name
the group of sages who come to the king and teach him
the chief of the sages, who speaks the sermon
the sky-travelling sages called Jagadabhinandana, probably the same sages
the people who hear the sermon
the Vidyadhara king's young daughter who takes the vow
the Jain god, here addressed in the girl's hymn

191.reading: The sages, their own duties fully done and now mountains of virtue, look to the war-proud king and are eager to pour the rain of dharma on him.
191.nuance: The rain-of-dharma image has the teaching fall on the hearer unasked by any gift from him; the sages' eagerness, not the king's request, begins the sermon (the king asks in 197).
191.event: The sages, having finished their rite, turn to the king wishing to teach him dharma.

192.reading: Wherever these sages sit there appear the south wind, a fine drizzle of honey, an ever-fresh cool ashoka tree and a shining disc of moonstone.
192.nuance: The verse lists the signs that mark a sage's seat; the ashoka (பிண்டி) is the Jain holy tree in the other Jain epics, but the verse itself does not name any faith.

193.reading: When the sages take their place on the three-tiered platform of the Victor's shining city, the spear-bearing king goes to them and sets their feet upon his head.
193.event: The king goes to the sages on the three-tiered platform and lays their feet on his crown.

194.reading: The sages bless the lord of the water-rich land and bid him sit, and he takes his seat amid women in fine cloth and jewelled girdles.
194.nuance: The king is called by his land (பழன நாடன்) and not by name; line 4 calls him faultless (ஏசிடை இலாதவன்) just as he comes to hear teaching on faults.
194.event: The sages bless the king and tell him to be seated; he sits among his attendant women.

195.reading: The sword-bearing king bows his jewelled crown to the sages and blesses them.
195.nuance: Lines 1-3 compare his shoulders to the lotus-seated goddess and a long necklace; the construction is hard and the sense of the comparison is a guess.
195.event: The king bows his crown to the sages and gives praise.

196.reading: The king looks at the chief of the sages and says he has one sweet thing to ask of him, and the sage answers him kindly.
196.nuance: Who says 'அடிகள்' and who asks the favour in lines 1-2 is not marked in the text; reading the king as the one who speaks first fits the sage's reply in 197.
196.event: The king addresses the chief sage, who replies gently.

197.reading: The sage says what is in the king's mind: he wants the old sweet word that cuts the bond of deeds, and the king folds his hands in eager assent.
197.event: The sage names the king's wish for the teaching, and the king joins his hands.

claims.claim: the ancient teaching is a sweet word that cuts the enemy-deeds that cling

198.reading: From the seed of lacking true knowledge there spring cruel helpless deeds which, when they ripen into harsh pain, leave living beings weary through a garland of births too long to reckon.
198.nuance: The verse names the seed as absence of true knowledge (மெய்யறிவிலாமை), not craving; lines 3-4 are tightly packed and the exact construction of the last line is uncertain.

claims.claim: lack of true knowledge is the seed from which harmful deeds grow
the births that deeds produce form a chain of suffering whose length cannot be reckoned

199.reading: Driven by their deeds, beings do further deeds from the fruit of the first, die in pain and are born again, and sink in suffering until they reach the refuge that bars the low births.
199.nuance: The refuge (சார்வு) is not yet named here; the next verse supplies it. The word is not the Buddhist சார்பு (dependent arising) of the Manimekalai.

claims.claim: deeds compel new action, and the fruit of one deed breeds further deeds
beings keep suffering through births until they reach a refuge that stops the fall

200.reading: The sage names the refuge: the feet of the one who stands beyond all beginning, whom the lords of enlightenment praise in meditation, as the cure for great suffering.
200.nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard: காதியம் looks like the four destroying deeds of Jain teaching, and போதியங் கிழவர் is a phrase other traditions use for those of the bodhi tree, here read as masters of enlightenment.

claims.claim: the feet of the Lord who stands beyond beginning are the one refuge that ends great suffering

201.reading: The sage tells the king to hold fast to what the Lord laid out: discerning true things, the knowledge that grows on them and conduct kept faithful to the text.
201.nuance: The verse names three things in turn; whether the poet means the Jain triad of right faith, knowledge and conduct is a reading, as the verse does not number them. Verse 203 speaks of three nectars.

claims.claim: true seeing, knowledge and conduct faithful to the scripture are the means the Lord taught

202.reading: The end of these is a state free of disease, age and the pain of births, with a shining form the world praises and a limitless, unfailing bliss, which those who are full of these things reach.
202.nuance: The verse says the released keep a form (உருவம்) and bliss; it does not say they join a god. Line 4 reads மற்ரவை, likely a slip for மற்றவை.

claims.claim: release is a state without disease, age or pain, with a shining form and unfailing bliss
those who fulfil the three means attain it

203.reading: Hearing the three nectars that cut hard suffering taught well, the people, lit by wide knowledge that tears the darkness of evil deeds, grow clear in heart as if freed from sin.
203.nuance: The 'three nectars' (அமிர்தவைகள் மூன்றும்) most likely refer back to the three things of verse 201, but the verse does not say so. The verse says the people were as if without sin (ஒத்தார்), not that they were.
203.event: The assembled people hear the teaching and are cleared of heart as if of sin.

claims.claim: hearing the true teaching lets the light of knowledge split the darkness of evil deeds

204.reading: The sage's jewel-bright words, which end the sins they tell of, bring the king to right vision, and his own one too takes up a great vow.
204.nuance: காட்சி (sight, vision) is read here as the right seeing of the Jain triad. உரிமை (one's own, dear one) is taken as the daughter of 205, but the verse does not say who it is.
204.event: The king reaches clear sight through the sage's words and a dear one of his takes a great vow.

claims.claim: a true teacher's words remove the sins they speak of and bring right seeing

205.reading: The king's young daughter bows, rises shining after drinking their sweet word, resolves on a vow and thinks how to finish it with greatness.
205.nuance: The verse does not name her; she is the girl born as Sayampavai in verse 150, which this chapter does not repeat.
205.event: The king's young daughter bows to the sages and takes a vow.

206.reading: Wearing a garland of honeyed cool flowers, the king bows to the sages' feet, circles the god's shining city in the right-hand way and goes.
206.event: The king bows to the sages, circles the shrine city and leaves.

207.reading: The king, guarded by young men with spears, goes back to his own city.
207.nuance: Lines 1-2 say something of women's minds and the love-god's place in them, but the construction is not clear and the link to the king's return is a guess.
207.event: The king goes back to his own city.

208.reading: After the king and the lords of the inner city have gone, the sky-travelling sages called Jagadabhinandana praise the Lord again and leave through the sky in a blaze of light.
208.nuance: The sages named here are likely the same ones who taught the king, but the verse does not say so.
208.event: The sky-travelling sages worship the Lord and depart through the sky.

209.reading: By the vow she has taken, the creeper-haired girl comes to a flame-like glow that shines, like a banner of fire on a mansion.
209.nuance: Lines 1-2 pile images (a flame-banner, the shadow of mansion banners) and the comparison is hard to resolve; the main sense, that the vow makes her glow, is clear.
209.event: The king's daughter shines with a new glow from her vow.

210.reading: Though the girl is as soft as she is, a vow set out as it should be is high, and nothing is hard for those who are spotless within.
210.nuance: The verse says it of her tenderness: a delicate girl can bear a hard vow, because what holds it up is a clean mind, not strength of body.

claims.claim: nothing is hard to those of spotless inner virtue

211.reading: Honoured even by Indra's world, her vow sheds its light and she grows, nourished as if by mantra and sweet ghee, into something like a spotless flame-banner in the sky.
211.nuance: The mantra and ghee image can be read as a figure for her glow rather than a literal rite; the verse does not describe a fire-offering.
211.event: The king's daughter keeps her vow and glows like a flame-banner.

212.reading: After she has kept the vow named Chakravalam well, the sweet-voiced girl comes to wish a great special worship of the god.
212.nuance: The vow's name matches the city's in verse 130, and the text does not link them. Line 1 reads சுடொரொளி, probably for சுடரொளி.
212.event: The girl completes her vow and sets out to hold a great worship.

213.reading: On the moonlit hill, over the crest, the king's daughter worships the god's shrine and praises it so that the gods' world marvels.
213.event: The king's daughter worships at the hilltop shrine and praises the god.

214.reading: The hymn addresses the Lord as the primal god who gave the rare scripture, the lord of the bodhi, who stood on the flower, and bows to his holy feet.
214.nuance: Line 3 repeats line 2's போதியங் கிழவனை and breaks the metre of the sense; the line may be damaged. The words பூமிசை ஒதுங்கினை are close in sense to Kural 3's மலர்மிசை ஏகினான், but share no words with it, so this is a link, not an echo. The speaker is taken to be the girl, from 213.

claims.claim: the primal Lord gave the rare scripture

links.note: Kural 351 says the joyless birth comes from a confusion that takes the unreal for real; Soolamani 198 says deeds grow from a seed of lacking true knowledge and ripen into pain through a chain of births.
links.teaches: The sage supplies a growth path (seed, deeds, ripening, rebirth) for the couplet's bare claim, while the couplet says what kind of knowledge fails.

gains.a: the missing true knowledge is made specific as seeing the unreal as real, a wrong seeing and not just an empty gap
gains.b: the confusion gains the steps by which it ends in birth: a seed that grows into deeds that ripen as pain

links.note: Kural 361 names craving as the seed that produces unceasing birth; the Soolamani's sage names lacking true knowledge as the seed of the deeds that bind.
links.teaches: Two Tamil teachers name different seeds of rebirth, so the root of bondage is a question of doctrine and is not common ground.

gains.a: its seed is set beside a rival one, so lack of knowledge is shown as one choice among Tamil answers
gains.b: the couplet's craving gets an older cause to answer, whether craving grows out of not knowing

links.note: Soolamani 199 has deeds breed deeds until a refuge is reached; Tirumanthiram 120 has a teacher make the seeds of births like seeds touched by fire, which will not sprout.
links.teaches: Both see rebirth as a growing seed; the Jain verse tells how the chain runs, the Saiva verse how it is cut at the root by a teacher.

gains.a: it gains a picture of how the chain can be stopped at the seed, which the sage only says is by reaching a refuge
gains.b: it gains the chain that the scorched seed stands against, deeds producing deeds through their fruit

links.note: Soolamani 200 makes the feet of the beginningless Lord the refuge from great suffering; Tirumanthiram 138 says the holy feet are Sivam, Sivaloka and the path, and a refuge for those clear within.
links.teaches: Both name the feet a refuge, but the Saiva feet are the goal and the way at once, while the Jain verse sets the refuge apart from the state it leads to, described in 202.

gains.a: the refuge is shown as a means only, as the goal is another thing, by contrast with feet that are also the goal
gains.b: the feet as goal and refuge together are shown as one answer among others, since a Jain verse names them only as a refuge

links.note: Soolamani 200 recommends refuge in the Lord's feet as the cure for suffering; Civaka Cintamani 380 shows Civakan going to the Wise One as a raft because an old deed drove him.
links.teaches: The sermon says why to take refuge and the story shows why someone does, adding that the going is itself moved by an old deed.

links.note: Kural 355 says knowledge is seeing the real in whatever thing; Soolamani 201 sets discerning true things as the first of three, followed by knowledge and conduct kept to the text.
links.teaches: The epic makes the couplet's seeing the start of a sequence that does not end until conduct is kept, not the whole of release.

gains.a: the discerning of true things is placed first and so not enough alone, it must be followed by conduct
gains.b: the couplet's seeing is given a place in a larger course ending in disciplined conduct

links.note: After taking refuge, Manimekalai's teacher begins on the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha; Soolamani 201 gives three things to hold after the refuge in 200: true seeing, knowledge and conduct.
links.teaches: Both sermons give threes after refuge, but the Buddhist three are what one goes to for refuge and the Jain three are what the follower must hold.

links.note: Soolamani 202 describes release as a shining form and limitless, unfailing bliss; Tirumanthiram 136 says the soul subsides into Sivam as salt returns to water.
links.teaches: The two release verses differ on whether the freed self keeps its own form and bliss or subsides into another, if the salt image is read as loss of separate being and the Jain 'shining form' as a kept one.

gains.a: release is shown as a state the freed self keeps as its own, since no one else is named for it to join
gains.b: the salt image meets a Tamil account in which the freed soul keeps form and bliss, so merging is not the only picture of release

links.note: Kural 352 says that for those of stainless sight darkness leaves and joy arises; Soolamani 203 has the light of knowledge from the sage's words split the darkness of evil deeds in the whole assembly.
links.teaches: The two verses use darkness and light, but the epic has the light come to a crowd from a teacher's words, while the couplet leaves it to one's own clear sight.

gains.a: the darkness is given as the darkness of evil deeds, and the light comes by hearing a teacher
gains.b: the bare word 'darkness', which commentators read as hell, ignorance or births, is shown in one reading as the darkness of deeds

links.note: Verse 205 has the king's daughter resolve on a vow and think how to finish it with greatness; verse 212 has her complete the vow of Chakravalam and then wish a great special worship.
links.teaches: The resolve at the sermon's end is kept here, and it grows into a second act, the worship, beyond the vow.

links.note: Kural 3 gives the Lord as the one who walked on the flower, at whose feet one arrives; Soolamani 214 gives the girl's hymn to the primal Lord who gave the scripture, who stood on the flower, at whose holy feet she bows.
links.teaches: The hymn uses a flower-footed epithet close to the couplet's and gives it to the Jain Lord with titles that name him, which the couplet does not.

gains.a: a familiar Tamil epithet for the flower-footed Lord is borrowed as a form of worship, so the girl's praise sits in a shared idiom
gains.b: the couplet's disputed 'one who walked on the flower' appears in a later Jain work applied to the Arhat, one data point on how the epithet was read

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken

source_issues: Verse 202 line 4 reads மற்ரவை, probably a slip for மற்றவை.
Verse 212 line 1 reads சுடொரொளி and line 2 நோன்புயர, likely letters misread; the sense is clear.
Verse 214 line 3 repeats போதியங் கிழவனை from line 2 and is short in sense; the verse may be damaged, and 'சேதியஞ் செல்வ' is unclear.
The cast id sayampavai for the king's daughter may differ from the id used in chapters 9 and 10, which were marked in parallel.
